title: The gamelan lesson
text:
Every Saturday morning, Bayu walked to Pak Hadi's house to learn the gamelan. The front room was filled with bronze instruments that glowed softly in the light from the window. Bayu's favourite was the saron, a row of thick metal bars that lay across a wooden frame like sleeping fish.

For three weeks Bayu had practised the same short tune. He struck each bar with a wooden mallet, then pressed his other hand on it to stop the sound. "Why must I do that?" he asked. "The next note will sound muddy if the last one is still ringing," said Pak Hadi. "A gamelan is not one loud player. It is many players who listen."

Bayu sighed. He wanted to play fast, like the older boys in the village band. Their hands moved in a blur, and the crowd always clapped. His own tune sounded slow and plain.

On the fourth Saturday, Pak Hadi invited Bayu to sit with the full group for the first time. There were drums, gongs, a bamboo flute and two women who sang. Bayu's palms felt damp. When the gong rang, he began, and for a few bars all went well. Then his mallet slipped and struck the wrong bar with a loud clang.

Nobody stopped. The drummer glanced across and gave a tiny nod, as if to say, "Carry on." Bayu pressed his hand on the bar, took a breath and found his place again. Soon he noticed something strange. His steady notes were the floor beneath the flute's flying tune. When he played evenly, the singers' voices rose more easily above him.

At the end, the big gong gave one deep note that seemed to hum inside his chest. Pak Hadi smiled. "You made a mistake and you did not run away," he said. "That is how a musician begins."

Walking home, Bayu tapped a slow rhythm on his knees. It no longer sounded plain. It sounded like part of something bigger.
